items.title: Preparation: Building a Pre-Game Routine
items.objective: The player will be able to follow a written pre-game checklist from the night before through the first pitch so that arriving at the field feels calm and ready.
items.summary: Being ready is a routine, not luck. Build a pre-game checklist for the night before, the morning of, and the first thirty minutes at the field.

video.note: The production video will show a player packing a bag the night before, arriving at the field and greeting the coach, jogging and stretching, going through the throwing warm-up, and taking a quiet breath before the first pitch.

explanation: A pre-game routine is a set of steps you do the same way before every game so that your body and mind know it is time to play. Players who have a routine arrive calm because nothing is a surprise: the bag is packed, the warm-up is familiar, and the first pitch arrives on schedule. Players without a routine spend the first inning looking for a batting glove and wondering if they are ready. The routine is how you answer that question before it is asked.

The routine starts the night before. Pack the bag with glove, cleats, hat, water bottle, a protective cup where required, sunscreen, and any batting gloves or your own helmet; set the uniform out; charge nothing except yourself by going to bed at a normal time. In the morning, eat the kind of familiar meal you would eat on any day a couple of hours before you play, and drink water during the day. This is not a diet plan; it is simply not trying anything new on game day.

At the field, arrive when the coach asks, usually 30 to 45 minutes before the first pitch. Greet the coach, put your gear where the team keeps it, and start moving: a jog, then dynamic stretches such as high knees, skips, and arm circles. Then the throwing warm-up, starting close and easy and backing up as the arm loosens, the same way every time. A few swings with a bat only in the area the league allows. Then sit for one minute, take a breath, and think about your job in the first inning: what you do if the ball is hit to you with nobody on base.

The last part of the routine is a focus word or short phrase that you say to yourself when the umpire says 'play ball'. It can be the same cue word you use for the next-pitch reset. The point is that your routine has a clear end, and after that moment you are playing, not preparing.

Parents help by protecting the routine, not running it. Leave on time, do not add last-minute instructions in the car, and let your child pack the bag themselves with a checklist on the wall. A forgotten glove once is a better teacher than a parent who packs the bag forever.
parentInstructions: Write the checklist with your child and post it where the equipment lives. Let your child check boxes; you only check the list the first few times.
Keep game-day meals and drinks ordinary and familiar. Game day is not the day to try a new food or a new sports drink.
Plan to arrive when the coach asks, not at first pitch. The warm-up is part of the game, not optional.
In the car, talk about anything except baseball instructions. Music, school, or a joke keeps the mind calm.
After the game, ask which part of the routine helped and which part got skipped. Adjust the checklist together.
If your child is nervous, the routine is the answer: 'You packed the bag, you warmed up, you are ready. Now go play.'
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: This lesson needs nothing. Build the checklist on paper, then rehearse arriving at the field, jogging, stretching, and shadow throwing in the yard without a ball.
steps: Divide a page into three sections: night before, morning of, and at the field.
Night before: list the bag contents one item at a time, the uniform, and bedtime. Have the player say why each item matters.
Morning of: list a familiar meal a couple of hours before, water through the day, and leaving on time.
At the field: list greet the coach, gear in its place, jog, dynamic stretches, throwing warm-up from close to far, a few swings where allowed, one quiet minute, and the focus word.
Walk through the at-the-field section in the yard with no ball: jog, stretch, shadow throws from short to long, then the quiet minute.
Rehearse the night-before section for real before the next game using the written checklist.
After the game, review the checklist and change anything that did not work. Keep the routine as short as possible while still complete.
Repeat for three games until the checklist is memorized, then keep it posted as a backup.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arriving at first pitch and skipping the warm-up.
commonMistakes.fix: Put the coach's arrival time on the checklist and plan backward from it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying a new food, drink, or piece of equipment on game day.
commonMistakes.fix: Game day is for familiar things only. Test anything new at practice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Parents packing the bag so the child never learns the routine.
commonMistakes.fix: Hand the checklist to the player. A forgotten item once teaches more than a reminder every week.

commonMistakes.mistake: A routine so long it causes stress.
commonMistakes.fix: Cut it to the items that matter. Short and repeatable beats long and perfect.

safety: The throwing part of the warm-up follows the warm-up throwing routine from the throwing lessons: start close and easy, back up gradually, and never throw hard with a cold arm.
Swings happen only in the area your league allows, with a helmet on, and with nobody within two bat lengths.
Water goes in the bag every time, and the routine includes drinking before the game begins, not just after.

progression.easier: A three-item checklist: bag packed, arrive on time, warm up with the team. Add items as they become habits.
progression.harder: The player writes and runs the full routine alone, including leading the team's dynamic warm-up when the coach asks.

items.title: Healthy Competition: Effort Over Outcome
items.objective: The player will be able to set three effort goals before a game or practice and score themselves on those goals afterward instead of on the scoreboard.
items.summary: Competing hard is good; judging yourself only by the score is not. Learn to set effort goals you control and to measure your day by them, with words parents can echo.

video.note: The production video will show a player and parent choosing three effort goals before a game, the player sprinting out a routine ground ball, and the two of them scoring the goals together afterward with the final score never mentioned.

explanation: Baseball is a game, and games have winners and losers. Wanting to win is healthy; it is why you practice. The problem comes when the score is the only way you judge yourself, because the score depends on the other team, your teammates, the umpire, and plain luck. You can play your best game of the year and lose. Effort over outcome means measuring yourself by the things you control and letting the score be the score.

Effort goals are specific actions you can do on purpose no matter what the other team does. Good ones are things like 'sprint to first base on every ball I hit', 'be in the ready position on every pitch', 'call for every fly ball near me', or 'cheer each teammate by name'. A bad effort goal is 'get two hits', because a hard-hit ball can land in a glove. Pick three before every game or practice and say them out loud to a parent or coach.

After the game, score your effort goals, not the game. Give yourself a two if you did it every time, a one if you did it most of the time, and a zero if you forgot. Six is a perfect day, and a perfect effort day can happen in a loss. Then pick one thing to try next time. This is how players get better: one controllable thing at a time.

Competing against yourself does not mean going easy. Play hard, run hard, and try to win every inning. The difference is what you say when it is over. 'We lost but I sprinted every ball and called every fly' is a true sentence that makes you want to play again. 'We lost so I was bad' is not true and makes you want to quit.

Parents have the most powerful voice here. Three sentences that work: 'I loved watching you play.' 'You ran hard on that ground ball.' 'What did you try today that was hard?' Avoid making 'Did you win?' the first question after a game, and avoid comparing your child to teammates. When the adults at home talk about effort, the child learns to measure effort.
parentInstructions: Before each game or practice, ask your child to tell you their three effort goals. Write them on a sticky note and keep it in the car.
During the game, notice the effort goals when they happen. A thumbs-up from the stands when your child sprints out a ground ball is enough.
After the game, score the three goals together before anyone mentions the final score or anyone's statistics.
Use the three sentences: 'I loved watching you play', 'You ran hard on that ground ball', and 'What did you try today that was hard?'
When your child is upset about a loss, let them be upset for a bit, then return to the effort scoreboard. Do not pretend the loss did not matter; show that it is not the only thing that matters.
Do not compare your child to a teammate or an older sibling. Compare them only to their own last game.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: This lesson needs nothing. Effort goals are set and scored with a conversation and a sticky note, at the field, at home, or in the car.
steps: Explain the difference between an outcome, something that depends on other people and luck, and an effort, something you can choose to do. Sort five examples together.
Brainstorm ten effort goals for hitting, fielding, baserunning, and the dugout. Cross out any that depend on results.
Pick three for the next game or practice and say them out loud to a parent or coach.
Play or practice. Parents and coaches watch for the goals and say nothing about results during play.
Afterward, score each goal zero, one, or two and add them up. Six is a perfect effort day.
Choose one goal to keep and one new goal to try next time.
Repeat for a month and look back at the scores. Effort scores that climb are the real sign of improvement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing effort goals that are really outcome goals, like 'get a hit'.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask, 'Can you do this even if the other team plays perfectly?' If not, it is an outcome.

commonMistakes.mistake: Scoring the goals only after wins.
commonMistakes.fix: Score every game and every practice, especially the losses. That is when the effort scoreboard matters most.

commonMistakes.mistake: Parents asking 'Did you win?' as the first question.
commonMistakes.fix: Make 'How did your three goals go?' the first question every time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Giving a two for every goal to be nice.
commonMistakes.fix: Honest scores teach more. A one with a plan to improve is better than a fake two.

cues: One thing to try next time
safety: Effort goals never include throwing more or harder, since pitch counts and arm care still apply; 'count my pitches' is a good effort goal.
Hustle goals like sprinting to first are done with the same running-through-the-bag rules taught in baserunning lessons so that effort never means playing unsafely.

progression.easier: One effort goal per game, scored with a simple yes or no.
progression.harder: The player sets goals for a whole week of practices and games, tracks them in a notebook, and explains to the coach which goal has improved most.
